hook.situation: It's your first day at a Korean workplace or language-exchange group. Someone hands you a name card, points to a menu or book, and asks simple identity questions. You want to ask 'What is this?' and introduce your name, country, and job. You know a few Korean words — but how do you actually build a sentence that says what something IS? This chapter gives you the most useful two-word engine in Korean.
objectives: Use 이에요 after a noun ending in a consonant and 예요 after a noun ending in a vowel
Ask 이건 뭐예요? (What is this?) and answer with N이에요/예요
Use 은/는 to set the topic of a sentence, including the contrast meaning
hook.whyItMatters: N이에요/예요 is the 'is' of Korean — it builds every sentence that identifies, names, or defines something. You will use it within the first minute of any real Korean conversation. And 은/는 is not just grammar: it is how Korean tells the listener what the sentence is about. Miss this and your Korean sounds like a word list. Master it and your sentences feel complete.

grammarNotes.title: N이에요/예요 — The 'Is' of Korean
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 이에요/예요 as a LABEL MAKER. You pick up any noun, press the button, and out comes a sticker that reads: '[noun] is.' The only choice is which sticker roll to load: the 이에요 roll (for nouns that end with a final consonant — they need the 이 connector) or the 예요 roll (for nouns ending in a vowel — they attach directly). One machine, two rolls, infinite labels.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in consonant (받침) + 이에요 / Noun ending in vowel + 예요

examples.note: 메뉴 ends in the vowel ㅜ → use 예요 (no connector needed)
학생 ends in the consonant ㅇ (받침) → use 이에요 (이 acts as connector between the consonant and 에요)
커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ → 예요 attaches directly
선생님 ends in 받침 ㅁ → 이에요; the 이 bridges the final consonant to 에요
지도 ends in vowel ㅗ → 예요; no bridging consonant needed

contrastPairs.explanation: 빵 ends in the final consonant ㅇ (받침) → 이에요. 커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ → 예요. Same structure, same meaning — only the connector changes based on what the noun ends in.
학생 ends in consonant 받침 → 이에요. 의사 ends in vowel → 예요. Always check the very last letter of the noun — not the last syllable block.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers sometimes want to use 예요 everywhere because it sounds shorter. But 예요 can only follow a vowel-ending noun. 학생 ends in the final consonant ㅇ, so it needs 이에요. The learner habit is simple: check the final sound first, then choose 이에요 or 예요.

exceptions: 이에요 and 예요 are the polite present tense forms. The plain/intimate form is 이야/야 — you will hear 학생이야 between close friends.
The question form is identical — just add a rising intonation: 학생이에요? = Are you a student?
이에요 and 예요 attach to nouns only. For adjectives like 배고프다 (to be hungry), use an adjective ending such as 배고파요, not 예요.

grammarNotes.title: 은/는 — The Topic Marker
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 은/는 as a SPOTLIGHT on a stage. When you put 은/는 after a word, you shine the spotlight directly on it and say to the audience: 'This is what we are talking about right now.' Everything else in the sentence is what you say about that spotlit topic. The rule for which to use mirrors the label maker: 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in consonant (받침) + 은 / Noun ending in vowel + 는

examples.en: I am American. (As for me, I am American.)
examples.note: 저 ends in vowel ㅓ → 는; 는 spotlights 저 (me) as the topic of the whole sentence
이건 is 이것 + 은 contracted → 은 marks 이것 as the topic; ends in consonant ㅅ → 은

examples.ko: 저는 서울 사람이 아니에요. 부산 사람이에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun seoul sarami anieyo. busan saramieyo.
examples.en: I am not from Seoul. I am from Busan.
examples.note: 는 here carries a contrast meaning: 'As for ME (not someone else)' — 은/는 often implies 'but others may differ'

examples.en: As for your name, what is it? (What is your name?)
examples.note: 이름 ends in consonant ㅁ → 은; spotlighting 이름 (name) as the topic of the question
한국어 ends in vowel ㅓ → 는; the speaker is setting Korean as the topic and commenting on it

b.en: I am also a student. (also: me too)

contrastPairs.explanation: 은/는 sets the topic. 도 means 'also/too.' They are not interchangeable — 저는 introduces me as the topic of conversation; 저도 adds me to a list already mentioned.

a.en: Coffee, I like. / As for coffee, it's good.

b.en: Coffee is good. (coffee is the one that is good)

contrastPairs.explanation: 은/는 marks the topic (what we are talking about). 이/가 marks the subject (the grammatical actor). With 은/는 there is often a contrast or emphasis feel — 'coffee in particular.' With 이/가 it is a neutral statement of fact. This distinction is covered more deeply in Chapter 4.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers sometimes try to stack words in English word order: subject first, then 이에요 attached to the subject, then the noun. In Korean the topic marker 은/는 must come immediately after the topic noun, and 이에요/예요 comes at the very END of the sentence — always. Korean sentences consistently end with the verb or copula, never in the middle.

exceptions: 은/는 can replace the subject particle 이/가 or the object particle 을/를 when you want to topicalize that noun: 밥은 먹었어요 (As for rice, I ate it) — 밥 is the object but it is topicalized with 은
은/는 carries a subtle contrast: '저는 학생이에요' implies 'as for me (others may differ).' In a first introduction this contrast is mild, but be aware it exists.
이건 (이것은, contraction) and 그건 (그것은) are very common contracted topic forms — these sound more natural than the full form in speech

exampleSentence.note: 저 ends in a vowel, so the topic marker is 는. Use 저 with strangers and adults; 나 is casual.
이름 ends in consonant ㅁ → topic marker 은; 민수 ends in vowel ㅜ → 예요.
대학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요; 대학 (university) + 학생 (student)
선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; 님 is a respectful suffix — never drop it when addressing a teacher
의사 ends in vowel ㅏ → 예요; 제 is the possessive form of 저 (my)
회사원 ends in consonant 받침 ㄴ → 이에요; 회사(company) + 원(member/worker)
나라 ends in vowel ㅏ → would take 예요 when used as the sentence topic; 어느 = which
사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; [country] + 사람 is the standard pattern for nationality
이건 = 이것 + 은 (contracted); 이것 = this thing, 은 = topic marker; used constantly in real speech — more natural than 이것은
뭐 ends in vowel → 예요; 뭐 is the spoken/colloquial form of 무엇 (what)
아니에요 is the negative of 이에요/예요; the noun before it takes 이/가 (subject marker): 일본 사람이 아니에요
제 is the possessive form of 저 (polite 'I'); 내 is the possessive of 나 (casual 'I') — use 제 in formal/polite situations
직업 ends in consonant 받침 ㅂ → if the answer uses it as topic: 직업은; as subject in the question: 직업이
한국어 ends in vowel ㅓ → 예요. Use this when identifying a word, sentence, label, or class as Korean.
영어 describes the kind of teacher; 선생님 is the final noun, and it ends in ㅁ → 이에요.

exampleSentence.en: I'm Minjun. Nice to meet you!
exampleSentence.note: 반갑습니다 is formal; 반가워요 is slightly less formal — both are appropriate when meeting someone for the first time
어느 is a modifier — it must be followed by a noun; unlike 어디 (where), 어느 modifies a noun directly

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon, a Korean office worker, meets Minho, a new foreign colleague, in the break room on his first day

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Hello! I'm Jiyeon. Nice to meet you for the first time.
lines.grammarNote: 저는 — 저 ends in vowel → 는; 지연이에요 — 지연 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: Hello! I'm Minho. I'm glad to meet you too.
lines.grammarNote: 민호예요 — 민호 ends in vowel ㅗ → 예요; 저도 — 도 means 'also/too,' not a topic marker

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Minho, what country are you from?
lines.grammarNote: 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; the question has the same form as the statement — only intonation changes

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 저는 호주 사람이에요. 제 나라는 호주예요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun hoju saramieyo. Je naraneun hojuyeyo.
lines.en: I'm Australian. My country is Australia.
lines.grammarNote: 호주 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 나라는 uses 는 because 나라 ends in a vowel, and 호주 ends in a vowel → 예요.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Oh, really? What is your job?
lines.grammarNote: 직업이 뭐예요? — 직업 takes subject marker 이 here (not topic marker 은); 뭐 ends in vowel → 예요

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I'm a designer. What about you, Jiyeon?
lines.grammarNote: 디자이너예요 — 디자이너 ends in vowel ㅓ → 예요; 씨는요? — 는 is the topic marker + 요 means 'and you?' — a natural way to return a question

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: I'm an office worker. This is my business card.
lines.grammarNote: 회사원이에요 — 회사원 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요. 이건 = 이것 + 은; 명함 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 감사합니다. 이건 제 명함이에요. 잘 부탁드려요!
lines.romanization: Gamsahamnida. Igeon je myeonghamieyo. Jal butakdeuryeoyo!
lines.en: Thank you. This is my business card. I look forward to working with you!
lines.grammarNote: 이건 제 명함이에요 repeats the chapter's object-identifying frame in a real exchange. 잘 부탁드려요 is a first-meeting set phrase.

readingText.title: 새 친구 소개 (Introducing a New Friend)
readingText.body: 엄마, 저 오늘 새 친구 생겼어요! 이름은 지수예요. 지수는 대학생이에요. 우리 학교 학생이에요. 지수 씨는 제주도 사람이에요. 저는 서울 사람이에요. 지수 씨의 꿈은 영어 선생님이에요. 정말 좋은 사람이에요!
readingText.bodyTranslation: Mom, I made a new friend today! Her name is Jisu. Jisu is a university student. She's a student at our school. Jisu is from Jeju Island. I am from Seoul. Jisu's dream is to be an English teacher. She is a really good person!

comprehensionQuestions.question: What is the new friend's name and where is she from?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 이름은 지수예요 (Her name is Jisu). 제주도 사람이에요 (She is from Jeju Island).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What is Jisu's dream job?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 꿈은 영어 선생님이에요 (Her dream is to be an English teacher). 선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 이에요/예요 forms in the text. For each one, explain why 이에요 or 예요 was chosen based on the noun it follows.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 지수예요 — 지수 ends in vowel ㅜ → 예요. 대학생이에요 — 대학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요. 학생이에요 — 학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요. 제주도 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 서울 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 영어 선생님이에요 — 선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 좋은 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

culturalNote.title: 명함 (Meongham) — Business Cards and First Meetings in Korea
culturalNote.body: When meeting someone in a Korean professional or semi-formal context, business cards (명함) are exchanged with both hands or with one hand supported by the other at the wrist — never one-handed or casually tossed. You receive the card with both hands, read it, and then place it respectfully on the table in front of you (never stuff it straight into a pocket). The exchange is usually accompanied by 잘 부탁드려요, which literally means 'I humbly ask for your care' but functions like 'I look forward to working with you.' Even social introductions follow a similar rhythm: name, hometown, and job are the first three pieces of information Koreans typically share. Knowing 저는 [name]이에요/예요 and 저는 [place] 사람이에요 will carry you through the first five minutes of almost any Korean introduction.

inlineExercises.explanation: 학생 ends in the final consonant ㅇ (받침). After a consonant, you must use 이에요 — the 이 acts as a phonetic bridge between the consonant and 에요. 예요 can only follow a vowel-ending noun, so 학생예요 is wrong.
커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ. After a vowel, 예요 attaches directly without any connector. If you chose 이에요, the 이 would create an awkward extra syllable — 커피이에요 — which sounds unnatural.
저 ends in the vowel ㅓ. After a vowel, the topic marker is 는. 은 is only used after a final consonant (받침). This is the same vowel/consonant rule as 이에요/예요 — one consistent rule governs both.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는 의사이에요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 의사 ends in the vowel ㅏ. After a vowel, you must use 예요, not 이에요. 의사이에요 sounds like adding an extra unnecessary syllable — 이 is only the bridge needed after a consonant. Correct: 저는 의사예요.

inlineExercises.hint: 이름 (name) + subject marker 이 + 뭐 (what) + 예요 (is). 뭐 ends in a vowel — which ending does that require?

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I am not Japanese.' Which sentence is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: The careful beginner form is [noun] + 이/가 아니에요. 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → use 이 before 아니에요. The first option says the opposite: 'I am Japanese.' The third option wrongly stacks 이에요 and 아니에요.

이건 is the contracted form of 이것 + 은 (이것은 → 이건). This is how native speakers actually say it — 이것은 뭐예요? is grammatically correct but sounds stiff. 이는 is not a standard form. The contraction 이건 is what you will hear in real conversation every time.

bullets: LABEL MAKER rule: consonant-ending noun + 이에요, vowel-ending noun + 예요 — check the very last letter of the noun
SPOTLIGHT rule: 은/는 marks what you're talking about (topic); consonant → 은, vowel → 는; 이건 (이것은) is the contraction you'll use most
Negative: [noun]이/가 아니에요 — the 이/가 before 아니에요 is required and beginners often drop it
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Chapter 4 introduces 있어요 and 없어요 — how to say something exists or you have it. You'll also meet 이/가, the subject marker, and start to see how it differs from 은/는. The 있다 vs. 없다 pair unlocks dozens of daily sentences immediately.
